items.title: [ArchDaily] UMG sede Antigua Guatemala / Atelier oficina de Arquitectura
items.content_html: The UMG Campus in Antigua Guatemala represents a critical case study in bridging traditional colonial architecture with massive institutional scale. Developed by ATELIER Oficina de Arquitectura, the primary challenge of this project was adapting a small-scale colonial design to a large-scale complex. We understood early in the planning phase that simply replicating historical facades is insufficient without considering the context and the diverse needs of a student complex.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Form Follows Formation: How Architecture Works with Geological Shapes
items.content_html: A canyon is a space no one designed. Its walls expose layers of rock deposited over millions of years, and the passage between them exists because water slowly wore that rock away. Glaciers shaped valleys in a similar way, leaving slopes behind as the ice retreated. Long before architects began shaping spaces, the Earth was already producing them.

items.title: [ArchDaily] From Asbestos to Fungi: Eight New Materials Made from Waste and Living Matter
items.content_html: Architecture is, above all, a material reality. The materials that surround us are the result of a chain of constructive, economic, aesthetic and, in more contemporary examples, environmental considerations. Decisions are shaped by available technology, manageable technique, time-related expectations and regulatory frameworks. To face the pressures on our built environment, those multidimensional conditions must change through what we call innovation: the tangible creation of new products and strategies with problem-solving capabilities. Matter is the general term for physical substance that has mass and takes up space. When matter is given a specific type, form, or useful application, it becomes material. Material transformation therefore requires going beyond recycling and reuse: combining existing matter to create new materials that open up new possibilities for construction. The research presented below suggests that demonizing existing materials is unnecessary as long as this capacity for innovation exists.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Dammed Between Energy and Water Scarcity: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and the Nile
items.content_html: Every large dam divides as much as it connects, and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam is no exception. A monumental feat of architecture and engineering, the mega-dam has brought everyone together, for better or worse, to interrogate who gets to declare sovereignty over the riches of the river, be it water or momentum, and to challenge colonial-era Nile treaties.

items.title: [ArchDaily] The City as a Quarry: Housing Transformation
items.content_html:
The City as a Quarry: Housing Transformation brings together representatives of the European Commission and the Government of Catalonia with European architects to explore how the renovation, reuse and transformation of existing buildings can help increase housing supply in response to the housing crisis and the climate emergency.

Curated by architects Marta Peris and José Toral of PERIS+TORAL Arquitectes, the event examines the conversion of offices and commercial premises, the renovation and extension of residential buildings, and the reuse of structures and materials. Discussions will address public policy, financing, regulation and architectural practice.

The event is part of the series Contemporary Catalan

items.title: [ArchDaily] Planned Overflow: How Singapore Balances Floods, Canals, and Public Space
items.content_html: At Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park in Singapore, a river does not occupy a fixed boundary. Under ordinary conditions, water moves through a naturalized channel bordered by grass, planting, and paths that bring visitors close to the river. During heavy rainfall, water spreads into the surrounding park, which is designed to accommodate flows beyond the capacity of the narrower channel. What appears to be a public landscape is also working infrastructure. Singapore's approach retains drainage engineering while assigning a wider role to the land around it.

items.title: [ArchDaily] How Material Choices Shape Contemporary Additions to Historic Buildings
items.content_html: Adding new floors on top of a historic building presents a challenge beyond accommodating additional space: how can a contemporary intervention respond to the character of an existing structure? Material selection plays an important role in establishing a relationship between different construction periods, whether the aim is to complement the existing building or create a more distinct architectural expression. The LH Residence in Varna, Bulgaria, designed by STARH, offers an example of how fiber cement can help relate a contemporary addition to a historic building.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Montana Farm / Estudio Balzano
items.content_html: Montana Farm is a boutique equestrian breeding and training facility located in Buenos Aires, Argentina, dedicated to the selective breeding and high-level training of show jumping horses. The project was conceived to integrate architecture, landscape, and the specific needs of horses within a contemporary equestrian complex, prioritizing animal welfare, functionality, and spatial quality.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Ombria Hotel and Apartments Loulé / PROMONTORIO
items.content_html: Quinta da Ombria is a property in the Algarve hinterland with 150 hectares. Surrounded by extensive citrus groves, fig and carob trees, small farms and villages, the dramatic landscape and the rich biodiversity of this mountainous estate comprise a watercourse and a series of archaeological remnants related to farming and its early waterworks. The resort comprises golf course, hotel and clubhouse, in addition to villas and other residential units.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Learning from Capitalism: How Postmodern Architecture Became the Language of American Business
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

In 1972, Robert Venturi, Denise Scott Brown, and Steven Izenour published Learning from Las Vegas, challenging architects to reconsider the underappreciated, largely dismissed commercial landscape in the United States. Their storied distinction between the "duck," a building whose form communicates its meaning, and the "decorated shed," an ordinary structure whose identity is conveyed through signs and symbols, questioned a widely accepted modernist assumption that architectural expression should emerge from form and function. By examining billboards, neon lights, casinos, and the commercial strips of Las Vegas, the authors argued that architecture should study the visual languages of American consumer culture.

items.title: 🔓 [Country Life] 'It is hard to imagine a more perfect realisation of Baillie Scott’s ideal of domestic harmony': The story of Church Rate Corner in Cambridge
items.content_html: Church Rate Corner in Cambridge —home of Michael Nedo and Gillian Moore —is a lovingly maintained house that perfectly captures the spirit of the Arts-and-Crafts Movement and the domestic ideals of the architect Baillie Scott. William Fawcett reports; photographs by Will Pryce.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Residential house in Vilnius / Architectural Bureau G.Natkevicius & Partners
items.content_html: The project was implemented in an exceptional location in Vilnius – the Aukštagiris Geomorphological Reserve. The protected forest environment and hilly terrain became the main axis of this architectural concept. The landscape dictated the position of the buildings on the plot, allowing for maximum use of natural light, opening up the most spectacular views through the windows, and maintaining a respectful, sustainable relationship with nature.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Legombang Treehouse / Cave Urban
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Legombang Treehouse reinterprets traditional Balinese architecture as a contemporary tropical family home, using reclaimed timber, passive design, and a treehouse-like structure woven around the site's existing trees. Designed by Cave Urban co-founder Jed Long for his own family, the house is located in Pantai Lembeng, Ketewel, Bali. As both architect and client, Jed had the opportunity to explore his own approach to tropical family living without the constraints of a conventional client brief.

items.title: [ArchDaily] La Joya / Veö estudio
items.content_html:
On a plot of land that rises thirteen meters (forty-three feet) from the street, "La Joya" House transforms the challenge of a steep slope into an architectural journey, revealing the landscape of San Agustinillo level by level.
The project emerged from a brief to develop three independent units: two small apartments intended primarily as rentals, and a larger residence for the owners' temporary stays. Instead of concentrating the program into a conventional volume, the steep topography offered an opportunity to fragment it and distribute it across different levels along the hillside. Consequently, each unit finds its own place within the site, maintaining privacy while enjoying a direct relationship with the sea.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Herdade da Matinha Country House / Sabrab
items.content_html:
🎨 🔭 ✏️

Between the cork oaks and the Vicentina Coast, Herdade da Matinha was born from an abandoned Alentejo estate, whose chimney still bears the date 1917. This rural tourism project, developed by SABRAB Architecture in collaboration with the owner Alfredo Moreira da Silva, starts from a simple principle: to make use of what already existed and add only what was necessary, with the same economy of means that has always characterized rural construction in the Alentejo region.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] The AI infrastructure race: I’ve seen this movie before
items.content_html:
Back in 2022, when the auto industry was fixated on autonomous vehicles, I was cofounder and chief technology officer at Luminar, where our lidar technology was helping enable the next generation of self-driving cars. Speaking at an automotive conference, I remarked how exciting it was to have a front-row seat to one of the most significant technological transformations in the industry’s history.

Afterward, an automotive executive pulled me aside.

“Jason,” he said, “you don’t have a front-row seat. You’re part of the show. What you’re doing for autonomy, and how you’re forcing us to think, is exactly what’s needed.”

That conversation stayed with me ever since, because it captured something larger than autonomous driving. When an industry is being transformed by technology, the companies that built the old infrastructure are not always the ones that define the new one. In autonomy, some of the companies that pushed furthest were technology companies like Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox; not the automakers that had dominated transportation for a century.

I believe we are watching the same pattern emerge again.

Today, I’ve shifted my focus from optics for autonomous vehicles to optical networking for AI infrastructure. And once again, technology companies are confronting infrastructure that was built for a different era. Rather than wait for traditional power and telecommunications providers to catch up, they are taking the problem into their own hands.

That is the shift that matters. The companies building artificial intelligence are no longer just customers of infrastructure. They are beginning to become infrastructure companies themselves.

Just as they did during the autonomy race, the technology companies aren’t waiting for the traditional infrastructure industries to solve the problem.

The benefits of urgency

When autonomous vehicles were supposed to be the next big thing, the tech innovators and the auto companies attacked the problem from different directions. Tech companies threw themselves into lidar (light detection and ranging), radar, computer vision, and AI software with genuine urgency.

Many of the traditional automakers approached it differently. They invested enormous sums—tens of billions of dollars collectively—through internal programs, acquisitions, and partnerships. Ford created Argo AI and later Latitude AI. General Motors built Cruise. Volkswagen invested heavily in Argo AI and Cariad. Toyota, Mercedes-Benz, and Nissan each launched major autonomous initiatives of their own. Despite these investments, many of the highest-profile programs were scaled back, reorganized, or shut down as the complexity of bringing true autonomous driving to market became clear.

Meanwhile, companies like Waymo and Zoox, born in the technology industry rather than the automotive industry, continued advancing because they reimagined the entire system around software, AI, and compute.

The result is visible on the roads today: Waymos and Zooxes that don’t come from Detroit.

Tech race 2.0

Having helped build one technological transformation from the inside, I’ve learned to recognize the early signs of the next one. I’m watching a similar game unfold again, though with different players and far higher stakes.

The driving force this time is AI. Hyperscalers, the Googles, Microsofts, Amazons and Metas of the world, are racing to build the data centers that will power the AI economy. Power has emerged as one of the defining constraints on AI infrastructure. These facilities are extraordinarily power hungry, and the grid isn’t keeping up.

Just as they did during the autonomy race, the technology companies aren’t waiting for the traditional infrastructure industries to solve the problem.

They’re investing directly in power generation, private optical networks, advanced cooling, and the technologies needed to connect geographically distributed AI campuses into what increasingly functions as a single AI factory.

Microsoft signed a 20-year power agreement that is helping make possible Constellation’s restart of Three Mile Island. Elon Musk has pursued natural gas generation for xAI’s data center campuses for much the same reason. When a single AI campus can justify billions of dollars in dedicated energy investment, the economics of infrastructure begin to change, and the companies building AI begin to look a lot like infrastructure companies themselves. Texas has even moved toward requiring many new large data centers to bring their own generation capacity, a recognition that the grid alone cannot keep pace with AI’s growth.

None of this is because utilities are failing. They are doing exactly what society has asked them to do: provide reliable, affordable electricity within a highly regulated framework. Permitting, environmental review, transmission planning, and rate-case proceedings all take years. AI infrastructure is being deployed in months. The mismatch isn’t competence. It’s speed. While utilities work within those constraints, the hyperscalers are increasingly building around them.

Telecommunications is experiencing the same shift. Much of today’s carrier infrastructure was designed for an internet built around consumers, enterprises, and mobile devices. AI changes the traffic patterns entirely. Rather than wait for carriers to evolve, hyperscalers are building private optical networks between their own campuses and purchasing networking equipment directly from manufacturers. Once again, they’re becoming builders of infrastructure instead of merely customers of it.

A new generation of innovators is asking a fundamentally different question: What if the underlying architecture itself needs to change?

History rarely repeats itself exactly, but it often rhymes.

We can’t afford to play catch-up

This isn’t an argument for utilities or telecommunications providers to step aside. Quite the opposite. Their role will become even more important. But institutions built around long investment cycles, regulated returns, and legacy infrastructure cannot be expected to move at the pace of AI. The companies creating the demand are increasingly becoming the companies creating the infrastructure.

I’ve had the unusual privilege of helping build technology through two major infrastructure transitions. What I’ve learned is that technology almost always advances faster than the institutions surrounding it. Eventually those institutions adapt. But rarely before innovators have forced them to rethink what’s possible.

The show has already started. The question isn’t whether that infrastructure will change. It’s who will build it.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Eyes on the Street: Jane Jacobs’ Concept and Contemporary Residential Architecture in Brazil
items.content_html: The concept of "eyes on the street" is perhaps the most famous within architectural and urban literature when it comes to urban security. Jane Jacobs uses this expression to refer to people who - consciously or unconsciously - use public spaces or observe them from their homes, generating natural surveillance. A movement that, within our discipline, is encouraged both through quality public spaces and through the powerful relationship between the public and private created through building facades. Advocating for this daily control, Jacobs believes in a way of making architecture and cities that condemns excessive verticalization, reinforced by isolated buildings and single-use ones that deny contact with the street.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Lele Hotel / The Lab Evn
items.content_html: Located in Vayots Dzor, Lele Hotel is conceived as a direct response to the character and topography of its mountainous surroundings. Rather than imposing a separate architectural object on the landscape, the design seeks continuity with the terrain through its materiality, proportions, and relationship to the existing slope.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Buenos Aires Architecture City Guide: 31 Sites Between Heritage and the Contemporary
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Buenos Aires is a city of rich history and distinct atmospheres. There are many reasons to explore its architecture: the city is the result of a complex interplay of cultural factors shaped by a multitude of architectural styles and trends. Its streets and heterogeneous buildings define its inhabitants, reflecting an identity forged by its history.

items.title: [ArchDaily] CHYBÍK + KRIŠTOF Turns Aedes Into a Live Architecture Studio to Develop Four Berlin Projects
items.content_html: CHYBÍK + KRIŠTOF has opened Building the Existing City, an exhibition at Aedes Architecture Forum in Berlin that transforms the gallery into a working architecture studio. Running from October 23 to December 3, 2026, the exhibition centres on four architectural and urban design proposals for sites or urban situations in Berlin, selected through an open call. Over six weeks, visitors can follow the practice's research, discussions, and design work as the proposals develop, gaining insight into the processes through which architectural interventions are conceived in response to local conditions.
